PROP
37
CREATES LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Authorizes $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of purchase price of a newly constructed home priced below about $1.5 million. Borrowers must be California residents, occupy the home, meet income limits, and pay at least 3% down. Bonds repaid by mortgage payments, not State. Fiscal Impact: No direct state or local costs. Supporters: United Nurses Associations of California; California Conference of Carpenters; California State Treasurer Fiona Ma Opponents: None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would create a new homebuying assistance program. The state could sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund the program. Bonds would be paid back by homeowners’ payments on their home loans.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not be required to create a new homebuying assistance program.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Zero Taxpayer Cost-No Taxpayer Risk. Prop. 37 makes buying a home more affordable, keeping homeownership attainable for hardworking and middle-class Californians, with low-interest mortgages funded by private bond investors, NOT TAXPAYERS. Must be CA resident to qualify, meet income requirements, occupy home, make monthly payments, repay loan. Strict accountability/audits.
CON
NO ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 37 WAS SUBMITTED.
FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

# California’s Proposition 37 would let buyers put 3% down on a new home, with a state loan covering the other 17%
Prop 37, the "California Middle-Class Home Ownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026," is an initiative statute placed on the ballot by petition.
It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide and the best-polling of them: 61% yes to 35% no in PPIC's September survey.
...
## Proposition 37 leads 61% to 35% with Newsom, Becerra and Democrats in support and editorial boards split:
PPIC's September survey of likely voters, fielded September 4–10, found 61% yes, 35% no and 3% undecided, the strongest support for any of the 14 measures.
Democrats back it 76% to 20% and independents 62% to 35%, while Republicans oppose it 62% to 35%.
Renters support it 70% to 28% and homeowners 59% to 38%; voters under 35 back it 69% to 26% and those 55 and older 54% to 42%.
Five percent named it the measure they are most interested in.
UC Berkeley's September poll did not ask about it, and PPIC's October survey had not been released as of October 18.

# What's on California's ballot in the 2026 midterm election? A voter's guide to the statewide races
## Proposition 37: Creates a loan program for middle-income homebuyers
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund a state homebuying assistance program for eligible middle-income Californians purchasing newly built homes.
The program would provide fixed-rate loans covering up to 17% of a qualifying home's purchase price.
Eligible buyers would have to meet income requirements, occupy the home as their residence and make a down payment of at least 3%.
A yes vote would establish the program and authorize the bonds.
A no vote would prevent the state from being required to create it.
The measure's proponents say it would make homeownership more accessible without directly relying on taxpayer-funded bond repayments.
The bonds would be repaid through borrowers' mortgage payments.
No formal opposition argument was submitted against the measure, though at least one critic, the League of Women Voters, has said Proposition 37 would fail to confront racial barriers to wealth-building and lower overall costs for families.

# Proposition 37 would set aside $25 billion to help Californians buy new homes
California’s November ballot includes Proposition 37, proposing a down payment assistance program to help low- to middle-income Californians purchase newly constructed homes.
Proposition 37 would allow California’s Housing Finance Agency to borrow upwards of $25 billion to provide low-interest loans at 17% of a home’s value to potential homebuyers.

The home must be newly built, and eligible buyers can earn a maximum of twice their area’s median income.
For example, in the city of San Luis Obispo, buyers could not earn more than $147,000 annually to remain eligible, according to the Census Data.

Two new independent polls released days before the Nov. 3, 2026 election show California's proposed billionaires tax losing support, while a measure to make higher income tax rates permanent holds a steady majority.
The latest poll by the Institute of Governmental Studies at UC Berkeley found 42 percent of likely voters in favor of Proposition 40 and 50 percent opposed, with 8 percent undecided.
It would need majority support to pass.
...

# Is California’s Proposed Billionaire Tax in Trouble? New Polls Find Bad News
A proposal to tax California’s billionaires to fund healthcare is trailing in two public, nonpartisan polls released this week, surveys that also found strong opposition to a separate ballot measure that would require voters to show identification at the polls.
Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time, 5% tax on the overall wealth of the state’s billionaires, was tracking below the majority needed to pass in polls from both UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies and the Public Policy Institute of California.
...
Proposition 39, the voter ID initiative, was also trailing by 20 points in the IGS poll, with just 37% of likely voters saying they were voting yes and 5% undecided.

# California Prop. 40, the ‘Billionaire Tax,’ holds lead in new UC Berkeley IGS Poll
*The new poll finds that likely voters in the Nov. 3 election are split along partisan lines on ballot measures to tax the richest Californians and to require an official ID when voting.*
...
Proposition 40, the controversial measure to impose a one-time tax on California billionaires, has the support of 48% of likely voters ahead of November’s election, with 41% opposed, according to a new report by the UC Berkeley IGS Poll.
The poll, released Friday Aug. 14, also found that likely voters are leaning against Proposition 39, which would establish strict ID requirements at the polls: 51% opposed to it and 42% in favor.
...
Among Republican likely voters, 93% favored Proposition 39’s ID requirements.
Among Democrats, 80% would vote no.
Among likely voters with no party preference, 54% opposed  Proposition 39.
...
The poll was conducted online in English and Spanish from Aug. 3 to Aug. 9 among 4,207 registered voters throughout California.
The poll has a margin of error of 2.5 percentage points.

Proposition 37 : State loans for middle-income buyers of new homes
Published September 29, 2026 · Updated November 2, 2026
Proposition 37 would let the California Housing Finance Agency sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund a new down payment loan program. Loans could cover up to 17% of the price of a newly built home, and buyers would put down at least 3%. Buyers must live in the home, be state residents and earn no more than twice their area's typical income. Homeowners' loan payments, not the state, would repay the bonds.
Summary by CityHallPass , not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: California Official Voter Information Guide: Proposition 37 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/).
Results
Polls close at 8 p.m. Pacific on Nov. 3. First results appear here after that.
At a glance
Proposition 37
Bond limit $25 billion in revenue bonds, repaid by borrowers
Loan size Up to 17% of the price; buyer puts down at least 3%
Top price in LA County About $1.56 million in 2026 (our calculation from federal loan limits)
Who can borrow One-year state residents, living in the home, earning up to 200% of area median income; first-time buyers not required
Cost to taxpayers No direct state or local cost (Legislative Analyst)
Money raised, Jan. 1, 2025 to Nov. 1, 2026 For: $28.0 million, including $3.9 million in late contributions after Oct. 17. Against: no committee
Largest donors California Association of Realtors committees, $18.76 million; Building a Better California, $6 million
Latest public poll PPIC, Oct. 16-22: 65% yes, 32% no (likely voters)
Each figure is sourced in the sections below. Money figures are our totals from the committees' state campaign reports.
Details and source links: Polls , Money for and against , What it costs , Sources .
What does a yes vote on Proposition 37 mean?
The state would create a new homebuying assistance program. The state could sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund the program. Bonds would be paid back by homeowners' payments on their home loans.
What does a no vote on Proposition 37 mean?
The state would not be required to create a new homebuying assistance program.
What would Proposition 37 cost?
The Legislative Analyst says there would be no direct state or local costs, because homebuyers' payments would repay the bond investors. How big the program gets depends on investor demand, how the loans compare with other options and whether it leads to more building and buying.
What it means for the City of LA
Homes in Los Angeles County would qualify up to a price of about $1.56 million, 125% of the county's 2026 federal conforming loan limit of $1,249,125 (our calculation). Only newly built or newly converted homes sold to their first buyer qualify. The City's own down payment programs serve first-time buyers and lower incomes; Prop. 37 would reach households earning up to twice the area median income. The Legislative Analyst finds no direct cost to the City or any local government.
The details
Official title Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes. Initiative Statute.
Type Initiative statute, placed on the ballot by petition signatures
Votes needed to pass Simple majority (more than 50% yes) of votes cast statewide
The question on your ballot
Authorizes $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of purchase price of a newly constructed home priced below about $1.5 million. Borrowers must be California residents, occupy the home, meet income limits, and pay at least 3% down. Bonds repaid by mortgage payments, not State. Fiscal Impact: No direct state or local costs. Supporters: United Nurses Associations of California; California Conference of Carpenters; California State Treasurer Fiona Ma Opponents: None submitted
What would change
Today If Proposition 37 passes
State down payment help The California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) runs a few down payment loan programs for low- and moderate-income buyers (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm)). Its Dream For All program lent up to $150,000 or 20% of the price to first-time buyers, with about $150 million to $200 million for its 2026 round and 14,000 applicants, the Orange County Register reported (OC Register (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/05/15/14000-apply-for-californias-housing-down-payment-program/)) A new “middle-class home ownership loan” funded by up to $25 billion in CalHFA revenue bonds (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm); text, Sec. 51515.06 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5))
Loan terms Not applicable A fixed-rate second mortgage for up to 17% of the price, behind the buyer’s first mortgage. The buyer puts at least 3% down from their own money. CalHFA sets the rate and terms at levels that repay the bonds and costs (text, Sec. 51515.05(b)-(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5); Sec. 51515.04 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3))
Who can borrow Not applicable California residents of at least one year who live in the home and earn no more than 200% of area median income for their family size. There is no first-time-buyer rule (text, Sec. 51515.01(a) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Which homes Not applicable New homes, townhomes, condos or manufactured homes, or units converted from nonresidential buildings, sold to their first buyer. The price may not exceed 125% of the county’s federal conforming loan limit (text, Sec. 51515.01(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3))
Lender fees Not applicable Origination fee capped at 0.5% or $290, whichever is greater. No prepayment penalty. Borrowers can ask to defer interest in a hardship (text, Sec. 51515.04 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=4))
Construction defect claims State law sets building standards and a process homeowners must follow before suing a builder (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm)) Builders who opt into a “qualified builder option” accept labor standards and liability for subcontractors’ wage violations. In return, their homes get different defect rules: builders may deal directly with owners, get releases after repairs and seek dismissal if owners stall for 120 days. Attorney contingency fees in defect cases over any qualifying home are capped at 30% unless a court allows more (text, Secs. 51515.02 and 51515.04(e) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=4))
Oversight Not applicable An independent annual audit of the program (text, Sec. 51515.05(g) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5))
Changes later Not applicable The Legislature may amend the act by more than a 60% vote of each house if the change furthers its purposes (text, Sec. 3 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5))
Each bond must state that it is not a debt of the State of California and is payable only from program funds (text, Sec. 51515.06(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5)). The measure does not set an interest rate for borrowers.
What it would mean in the City of Los Angeles
Price limit. The 2026 federal conforming loan limit for a one-unit home in Los Angeles County is $1,249,125 (FHFA (https://www.fhfa.gov/document/d/cll/fullcountyloanlimitlist2026_hera-based_final_flat.csv)). At 125% of that, a qualifying home could cost up to about $1,561,406, and a 17% loan on a home at that price would be about $265,439 (our calculations). The limit changes each year with the federal figure (text, Sec. 51515.01(b)(2) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3)).
New homes only. Resales do not qualify. Only new construction and conversions of nonresidential buildings sold to their first buyer do (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3)).
Compared with City programs. The City’s Moderate Income Purchase Assistance program lends up to $115,000 to first-time buyers, requires 1% down and a 660 credit score, and takes a share of the home’s appreciation (LA Housing Department (https://housing.lacity.gov/housing/help-moderate-income-first-home-buyers)). The Measure ULA-funded Homeownership Opportunities Program is limited to households at or below 80% of area median income (LA Housing Department (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula-homeownership)). Prop. 37 would reach households up to 200% of area median income and would not require a first purchase (text, Sec. 51515.01(a) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2)).
Cost. The Legislative Analyst finds no direct state or local cost (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm)).
Signatures. Los Angeles County supplied 253,493 of the 918,358 raw petition signatures, about 28% (our calculation from the Secretary of State random sample count (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/1990-finalrandomsample-04-22-26.pdf)).
We found no City of Los Angeles analysis or position on the measure as of Sept. 30, 2026.
How it got on the ballot
Oct. 21, 2025: The Attorney General issued the petition’s title and summary. The proponent is Robert M. Hertzberg (Secretary of State, eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)), whom the Mercury News describes as a former Los Angeles assemblymember (Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/21/housing-ballot-measure-california-election/)).
Nov. 18, 2025: The campaign reported 25% of the signatures needed (Secretary of State, eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)).
Feb.-March 2026: Petitions with 918,358 raw signatures were filed with the counties (random sample count (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/1990-finalrandomsample-04-22-26.pdf)).
April 21, 2026: The random sample projected 715,233 valid signatures, more than 110% of the 546,651 needed, and the measure became eligible (random sample count (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/1990-finalrandomsample-04-22-26.pdf); Secretary of State, eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)).
Vote needed. A majority of votes cast statewide (Cal. Const., Art. II, Sec. 10 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2010.&article=II)).
Related measure. Proposition 1 on the same ballot is an $11.25 billion general obligation housing bond, repaid from the state General Fund, that includes about $1 billion for homebuyer assistance, the Mercury News reported (Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/21/housing-ballot-measure-california-election/)). Prop. 37’s conflict clause covers only another measure that authorizes revenue bonds for middle-class housing loans (text, Sec. 6 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=6)). See our Proposition 1 (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/measures/prop-01) page.
What each side says
In the state voter guide. The argument in favor was signed by Danny Curtin of the California Conference of Carpenters, Fiona Ma as a board member of CalHFA and David West of the California State Commanders Veterans Council. No argument against was submitted, so there are no rebuttals (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/arguments-rebuttals.htm)). The argument says:
Down payments: with a statewide median home price above $930,000, a 20% down payment can mean saving “over $186,000.”
Cost: “ZERO COST TO TAXPAYERS,” because private bond investors fund the loans and borrowers repay them.
Construction: helping buyers of new homes “will help accelerate construction.”
Consumer terms: “below-market, fixed-rate loans,” limits on lender fees and no prepayment penalty.
Arguments are the opinions of their authors and have not been checked for accuracy by any official agency (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Outside the guide.
Hertzberg said the goal is “to create generational wealth” and to help renters become owners. Proponents say it would lead to more than 190,000 new homes (Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/21/housing-ballot-measure-california-election/)).
The League of Women Voters of California opposes it, faulting the lack of clarity on rates and the absence of a first-time-buyer priority: “Prop. 37 does not meet that test” (Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/21/housing-ballot-measure-california-election/)).
KQED’s guide quotes the No argument that it “makes the state of California one of the biggest mortgage lenders in America overnight” and that “taxpayers are left holding the bag,” and lists Assemblymember Carl DeMaio in opposition (KQED (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-37)).
David Garcia of UC Berkeley’s Terner Center, which takes no positions, said it could help residents who qualify for a mortgage but lack savings, while “creating demand for builders to build new housing” (Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/21/housing-ballot-measure-california-election/)).
Checking the main factual claims against official records.
Claim Who makes it What official records show
Zero cost to taxpayers Yes campaign The Legislative Analyst finds no direct state or local cost (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm)). The bonds must state they are not a state debt (text, Sec. 51515.06(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5))
Below-market, fixed-rate loans Yes campaign The loans must be fixed-rate (text, Sec. 51515.04(a) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3)). The text tells CalHFA to set rates “practical and favorable to applicants” while covering bond costs, but sets no rate (text, Sec. 51515.05(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5)). The Legislative Analyst says what the loans would cost buyers compared with other options is unknown (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm))
Will accelerate construction; 190,000 homes Yes campaign The Legislative Analyst lists “whether the program results in increased home construction and homebuying” as unknown (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm))
Annual audits Yes campaign The text requires an independent annual audit (Sec. 51515.05(g) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5))
Taxpayers are left holding the bag No side (KQED) See the first row. The Orange County Register editorial, which opposes the measure, says “taxpayers have no direct risk” and that bond investors bear losses on these second mortgages (OC Register (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/20/endorsement-no-on-proposition-37-a-risky-25-billion-housing-experiment/))
Who supports and opposes it
Supporters
California Conference of Carpenters, State Treasurer Fiona Ma, the California State Commanders Veterans Council and United Nurses Associations of California (ballot label (https://content.lavote.gov/docs/rrcc/documents/final-measures-appearing-on-the-ballot-8-20-2026-v-12.pdf); argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
State Controller Malia Cohen, quoted in the argument in favor, and the California Teachers Association, named there as a supporter (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
California Association of Realtors and the Veterans Affiliated Council; Democratic candidate for governor Xavier Becerra (KQED (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-37)).
California Democratic Party, whose executive board endorsed the $25 billion down payment program on Aug. 2 (LA Times (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2026-08-02/california-democratic-party-endorses-prop-40-billionaire-tax)).
Opponents
League of Women Voters of California (Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/21/housing-ballot-measure-california-election/)).
Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (KQED (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-37)). His Reform California committee reported $33,000 in independent spending against Prop. 37 through Oct. 25 (Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip)).
No opposition committee has registered (Secretary of State totals (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-37-creates-loan-program-middle-income-buyers-qualified-new-homes-initiative-statute); Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/21/housing-ballot-measure-california-election/)).
Editorial boards. The Daily News and Orange County Register recommend no (OC Register (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/20/endorsement-no-on-proposition-37-a-risky-25-billion-housing-experiment/); Daily News (https://www.dailynews.com/2026/09/20/endorsement-no-on-proposition-37-a-risky-25-billion-housing-experiment/)). The San Diego Union-Tribune also recommends no: “Voting no on Proposition 37 is a good start” (San Diego Union-Tribune, Oct. 2, 2026 (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/10/02/endorsements-props-2-37-wouldnt-yield-saner-state-budgets-more-housing/)). The Mercury News and East Bay Times editorial boards recommend no on Propositions 1 and 37. They say Prop. 37 is “a creative way to help Californians take on more debt” (Mercury News, Oct. 26, 2026 (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/26/endorsement-proposition-1-37-affordable-housing-crisis-november-3-general-election/))

Proposition 37 : State loans for middle-income buyers of new homes
Published September 29, 2026 · Updated November 2, 2026
Proposition 37 would let the California Housing Finance Agency sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund a new down payment loan program. Loans could cover up to 17% of the price of a newly built home, and buyers would put down at least 3%. Buyers must live in the home, be state residents and earn no more than twice their area's typical income. Homeowners' loan payments, not the state, would repay the bonds.
Summary by CityHallPass , not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: California Official Voter Information Guide: Proposition 37 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/).
Results
Polls close at 8 p.m. Pacific on Nov. 3. First results appear here after that.
At a glance
Proposition 37
Bond limit $25 billion in revenue bonds, repaid by borrowers
Loan size Up to 17% of the price; buyer puts down at least 3%
Top price in LA County About $1.56 million in 2026 (our calculation from federal loan limits)
Who can borrow One-year state residents, living in the home, earning up to 200% of area median income; first-time buyers not required
Cost to taxpayers No direct state or local cost (Legislative Analyst)
Money raised, Jan. 1, 2025 to Nov. 1, 2026 For: $28.0 million, including $3.9 million in late contributions after Oct. 17. Against: no committee
Largest donors California Association of Realtors committees, $18.76 million; Building a Better California, $6 million
Latest public poll PPIC, Oct. 16-22: 65% yes, 32% no (likely voters)
Each figure is sourced in the sections below. Money figures are our totals from the committees' state campaign reports.
Details and source links: Polls , Money for and against , What it costs , Sources .
What does a yes vote on Proposition 37 mean?
The state would create a new homebuying assistance program. The state could sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund the program. Bonds would be paid back by homeowners' payments on their home loans.
What does a no vote on Proposition 37 mean?
The state would not be required to create a new homebuying assistance program.
What would Proposition 37 cost?
The Legislative Analyst says there would be no direct state or local costs, because homebuyers' payments would repay the bond investors. How big the program gets depends on investor demand, how the loans compare with other options and whether it leads to more building and buying.
What it means for the City of LA
Homes in Los Angeles County would qualify up to a price of about $1.56 million, 125% of the county's 2026 federal conforming loan limit of $1,249,125 (our calculation). Only newly built or newly converted homes sold to their first buyer qualify. The City's own down payment programs serve first-time buyers and lower incomes; Prop. 37 would reach households earning up to twice the area median income. The Legislative Analyst finds no direct cost to the City or any local government.
The details
Official title Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes. Initiative Statute.
Type Initiative statute, placed on the ballot by petition signatures
Votes needed to pass Simple majority (more than 50% yes) of votes cast statewide
The question on your ballot
Authorizes $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of purchase price of a newly constructed home priced below about $1.5 million. Borrowers must be California residents, occupy the home, meet income limits, and pay at least 3% down. Bonds repaid by mortgage payments, not State. Fiscal Impact: No direct state or local costs. Supporters: United Nurses Associations of California; California Conference of Carpenters; California State Treasurer Fiona Ma Opponents: None submitted
What would change
Today If Proposition 37 passes
State down payment help The California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) runs a few down payment loan programs for low- and moderate-income buyers (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm)). Its Dream For All program lent up to $150,000 or 20% of the price to first-time buyers, with about $150 million to $200 million for its 2026 round and 14,000 applicants, the Orange County Register reported (OC Register (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/05/15/14000-apply-for-californias-housing-down-payment-program/)) A new “middle-class home ownership loan” funded by up to $25 billion in CalHFA revenue bonds (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm); text, Sec. 51515.06 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5))
Loan terms Not applicable A fixed-rate second mortgage for up to 17% of the price, behind the buyer’s first mortgage. The buyer puts at least 3% down from their own money. CalHFA sets the rate and terms at levels that repay the bonds and costs (text, Sec. 51515.05(b)-(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5); Sec. 51515.04 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3))
Who can borrow Not applicable California residents of at least one year who live in the home and earn no more than 200% of area median income for their family size. There is no first-time-buyer rule (text, Sec. 51515.01(a) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Which homes Not applicable New homes, townhomes, condos or manufactured homes, or units converted from nonresidential buildings, sold to their first buyer. The price may not exceed 125% of the county’s federal conforming loan limit (text, Sec. 51515.01(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3))
Lender fees Not applicable Origination fee capped at 0.5% or $290, whichever is greater. No prepayment penalty. Borrowers can ask to defer interest in a hardship (text, Sec. 51515.04 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=4))
Construction defect claims State law sets building standards and a process homeowners must follow before suing a builder (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm)) Builders who opt into a “qualified builder option” accept labor standards and liability for subcontractors’ wage violations. In return, their homes get different defect rules: builders may deal directly with owners, get releases after repairs and seek dismissal if owners stall for 120 days. Attorney contingency fees in defect cases over any qualifying home are capped at 30% unless a court allows more (text, Secs. 51515.02 and 51515.04(e) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=4))
Oversight Not applicable An independent annual audit of the program (text, Sec. 51515.05(g) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5))
Changes later Not applicable The Legislature may amend the act by more than a 60% vote of each house if the change furthers its purposes (text, Sec. 3 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5))
Each bond must state that it is not a debt of the State of California and is payable only from program funds (text, Sec. 51515.06(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5)). The measure does not set an interest rate for borrowers.
What it would mean in the City of Los Angeles
Price limit. At 125% of that, a qualifying home could cost up to about $1,561,406, and a 17% loan on a home at that price would be about $265,439 (our calculations). New homes only. Resales do not qualify. Only new construction and conversions of nonresidential buildings sold to their first buyer do (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3)).
Compared with City programs. The City’s Moderate Income Purchase Assistance program lends up to $115,000 to first-time buyers, requires 1% down and a 660 credit score, and takes a share of the home’s appreciation (LA Housing Department (https://housing.lacity.gov/housing/help-moderate-income-first-home-buyers)). Cost. The Legislative Analyst finds no direct state or local cost (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm)).
Signatures. Los Angeles County supplied 253,493 of the 918,358 raw petition signatures, about 28% (our calculation from the Secretary of State random sample count (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/1990-finalrandomsample-04-22-26.pdf)).

Proposition 37 : State loans for middle-income buyers of new homes
Published September 29, 2026 · Updated November 2, 2026
Proposition 37 would let the California Housing Finance Agency sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund a new down payment loan program. Loans could cover up to 17% of the price of a newly built home, and buyers would put down at least 3%. Buyers must live in the home, be state residents and earn no more than twice their area's typical income. Homeowners' loan payments, not the state, would repay the bonds.
Summary by CityHallPass , not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: California Official Voter Information Guide: Proposition 37 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/).

What does a yes vote on Proposition 37 mean?
The state would create a new homebuying assistance program. The state could sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund the program. Bonds would be paid back by homeowners' payments on their home loans.
What does a no vote on Proposition 37 mean?
The state would not be required to create a new homebuying assistance program.
What would Proposition 37 cost?
The Legislative Analyst says there would be no direct state or local costs, because homebuyers' payments would repay the bond investors. How big the program gets depends on investor demand, how the loans compare with other options and whether it leads to more building and buying.
What it means for the City of LA
Homes in Los Angeles County would qualify up to a price of about $1.56 million, 125% of the county's 2026 federal conforming loan limit of $1,249,125 (our calculation). Only newly built or newly converted homes sold to their first buyer qualify. The City's own down payment programs serve first-time buyers and lower incomes; Prop. 37 would reach households earning up to twice the area median income. The Legislative Analyst finds no direct cost to the City or any local government.
The details
Official title Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes. Initiative Statute.
Type Initiative statute, placed on the ballot by petition signatures
Votes needed to pass Simple majority (more than 50% yes) of votes cast statewide
The question on your ballot
Authorizes $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of purchase price of a newly constructed home priced below about $1.5 million. Borrowers must be California residents, occupy the home, meet income limits, and pay at least 3% down. Bonds repaid by mortgage payments, not State. Fiscal Impact: No direct state or local costs. Supporters: United Nurses Associations of California; California Conference of Carpenters; California State Treasurer Fiona Ma Opponents: None submitted
What would change
Today If Proposition 37 passes
State down payment help The California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) runs a few down payment loan programs for low- and moderate-income buyers (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm)). Its Dream For All program lent up to $150,000 or 20% of the price to first-time buyers, with about $150 million to $200 million for its 2026 round and 14,000 applicants, the Orange County Register reported (OC Register (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/05/15/14000-apply-for-californias-housing-down-payment-program/)) A new “middle-class home ownership loan” funded by up to $25 billion in CalHFA revenue bonds (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm); text, Sec. 51515.06 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5))
Loan terms Not applicable A fixed-rate second mortgage for up to 17% of the price, behind the buyer’s first mortgage. The buyer puts at least 3% down from their own money. CalHFA sets the rate and terms at levels that repay the bonds and costs (text, Sec. 51515.05(b)-(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5); Sec. 51515.04 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3))
Who can borrow Not applicable California residents of at least one year who live in the home and earn no more than 200% of area median income for their family size. There is no first-time-buyer rule (text, Sec. 51515.01(a) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Which homes Not applicable New homes, townhomes, condos or manufactured homes, or units converted from nonresidential buildings, sold to their first buyer. The price may not exceed 125% of the county’s federal conforming loan limit (text, Sec. 51515.01(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3))
Lender fees Not applicable Origination fee capped at 0.5% or $290, whichever is greater. No prepayment penalty. Borrowers can ask to defer interest in a hardship (text, Sec. 51515.04 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=4))
Construction defect claims State law sets building standards and a process homeowners must follow before suing a builder (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm)) Builders who opt into a “qualified builder option” accept labor standards and liability for subcontractors’ wage violations. In return, their homes get different defect rules: builders may deal directly with owners, get releases after repairs and seek dismissal if owners stall for 120 days. Attorney contingency fees in defect cases over any qualifying home are capped at 30% unless a court allows more (text, Secs. 51515.02 and 51515.04(e) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=4))
Oversight Not applicable An independent annual audit of the program (text, Sec. 51515.05(g) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5))
Changes later Not applicable The Legislature may amend the act by more than a 60% vote of each house if the change furthers its purposes (text, Sec. 3 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5))
Each bond must state that it is not a debt of the State of California and is payable only from program funds (text, Sec. 51515.06(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5)). The measure does not set an interest rate for borrowers.

Supporters
California Conference of Carpenters, State Treasurer Fiona Ma, the California State Commanders Veterans Council and United Nurses Associations of California (ballot label (https://content.lavote.gov/docs/rrcc/documents/final-measures-appearing-on-the-ballot-8-20-2026-v-12.pdf); argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
State Controller Malia Cohen, quoted in the argument in favor, and the California Teachers Association, named there as a supporter (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
California Association of Realtors and the Veterans Affiliated Council; Democratic candidate for governor Xavier Becerra (KQED (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-37)).

Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (KQED (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-37)). His Reform California committee reported $33,000 in independent spending against Prop. 37 through Oct. 25 (Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip)).

Proposition 37 : State loans for middle-income buyers of new homes
Published September 29, 2026 · Updated November 2, 2026
Proposition 37 would let the California Housing Finance Agency sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund a new down payment loan program. Loans could cover up to 17% of the price of a newly built home, and buyers would put down at least 3%. Buyers must live in the home, be state residents and earn no more than twice their area's typical income. Homeowners' loan payments, not the state, would repay the bonds.
Summary by CityHallPass , not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: California Official Voter Information Guide: Proposition 37 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/).
Results
Polls close at 8 p.m. Pacific on Nov. 3. First results appear here after that.
At a glance
Proposition 37
Bond limit $25 billion in revenue bonds, repaid by borrowers
Loan size Up to 17% of the price; buyer puts down at least 3%
Top price in LA County About $1.56 million in 2026 (our calculation from federal loan limits)
Who can borrow One-year state residents, living in the home, earning up to 200% of area median income; first-time buyers not required
Cost to taxpayers No direct state or local cost (Legislative Analyst)
Money raised, Jan. 1, 2025 to Nov. 1, 2026 For: $28.0 million, including $3.9 million in late contributions after Oct. 17. Against: no committee
Largest donors California Association of Realtors committees, $18.76 million; Building a Better California, $6 million
Latest public poll PPIC, Oct. 16-22: 65% yes, 32% no (likely voters)
Each figure is sourced in the sections below. Money figures are our totals from the committees' state campaign reports.
Details and source links: Polls , Money for and against , What it costs , Sources .
What does a yes vote on Proposition 37 mean?
The state would create a new homebuying assistance program. The state could sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund the program. Bonds would be paid back by homeowners' payments on their home loans.
What does a no vote on Proposition 37 mean?
The state would not be required to create a new homebuying assistance program.
What would Proposition 37 cost?
The Legislative Analyst says there would be no direct state or local costs, because homebuyers' payments would repay the bond investors. How big the program gets depends on investor demand, how the loans compare with other options and whether it leads to more building and buying.
What it means for the City of LA
Homes in Los Angeles County would qualify up to a price of about $1.56 million, 125% of the county's 2026 federal conforming loan limit of $1,249,125 (our calculation). Only newly built or newly converted homes sold to their first buyer qualify. The City's own down payment programs serve first-time buyers and lower incomes; Prop. 37 would reach households earning up to twice the area median income. The Legislative Analyst finds no direct cost to the City or any local government.
The details
Official title Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes. Initiative Statute.
Type Initiative statute, placed on the ballot by petition signatures
Votes needed to pass Simple majority (more than 50% yes) of votes cast statewide
The question on your ballot
Authorizes $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of purchase price of a newly constructed home priced below about $1.5 million. Borrowers must be California residents, occupy the home, meet income limits, and pay at least 3% down. Bonds repaid by mortgage payments, not State. Fiscal Impact: No direct state or local costs. Supporters: United Nurses Associations of California; California Conference of Carpenters; California State Treasurer Fiona Ma Opponents: None submitted
What would change
Today If Proposition 37 passes
State down payment help The California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) runs a few down payment loan programs for low- and moderate-income buyers (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm)). Its Dream For All program lent up to $150,000 or 20% of the price to first-time buyers, with about $150 million to $200 million for its 2026 round and 14,000 applicants, the Orange County Register reported (OC Register (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/05/15/14000-apply-for-californias-housing-down-payment-program/)) A new “middle-class home ownership loan” funded by up to $25 billion in CalHFA revenue bonds (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm); text, Sec. 51515.06 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5))
Loan terms Not applicable A fixed-rate second mortgage for up to 17% of the price, behind the buyer’s first mortgage. The buyer puts at least 3% down from their own money. CalHFA sets the rate and terms at levels that repay the bonds and costs (text, Sec. 51515.05(b)-(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5); Sec. 51515.04 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3))
Who can borrow Not applicable California residents of at least one year who live in the home and earn no more than 200% of area median income for their family size. There is no first-time-buyer rule (text, Sec. 51515.01(a) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Which homes Not applicable New homes, townhomes, condos or manufactured homes, or units converted from nonresidential buildings, sold to their first buyer. The price may not exceed 125% of the county’s federal conforming loan limit (text, Sec. 51515.01(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3))
Lender fees Not applicable Origination fee capped at 0.5% or $290, whichever is greater. No prepayment penalty. Borrowers can ask to defer interest in a hardship (text, Sec. 51515.04 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=4))
Construction defect claims State law sets building standards and a process homeowners must follow before suing a builder (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm)) Builders who opt into a “qualified builder option” accept labor standards and liability for subcontractors’ wage violations. In return, their homes get different defect rules: builders may deal directly with owners, get releases after repairs and seek dismissal if owners stall for 120 days. Attorney contingency fees in defect cases over any qualifying home are capped at 30% unless a court allows more (text, Secs. 51515.02 and 51515.04(e) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=4))
Oversight Not applicable An independent annual audit of the program (text, Sec. 51515.05(g) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5))
Changes later Not applicable The Legislature may amend the act by more than a 60% vote of each house if the change furthers its purposes (text, Sec. 3 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5))
Each bond must state that it is not a debt of the State of California and is payable only from program funds (text, Sec. 51515.06(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5)). The measure does not set an interest rate for borrowers.
What it would mean in the City of Los Angeles
Price limit. The 2026 federal conforming loan limit for a one-unit home in Los Angeles County is $1,249,125 (FHFA (https://www.fhfa.gov/document/d/cll/fullcountyloanlimitlist2026_hera-based_final_flat.csv)). At 125% of that, a qualifying home could cost up to about $1,561,406, and a 17% loan on a home at that price would be about $265,439 (our calculations). The limit changes each year with the federal figure (text, Sec. 51515.01(b)(2) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3)).
New homes only. Resales do not qualify. Only new construction and conversions of nonresidential buildings sold to their first buyer do (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3)).
Compared with City programs. The City’s Moderate Income Purchase Assistance program lends up to $115,000 to first-time buyers, requires 1% down and a 660 credit score, and takes a share of the home’s appreciation (LA Housing Department (https://housing.lacity.gov/housing/help-moderate-income-first-home-buyers)). The Measure ULA-funded Homeownership Opportunities Program is limited to households at or below 80% of area median income (LA Housing Department (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula-homeownership)). Prop. 37 would reach households up to 200% of area median income and would not require a first purchase (text, Sec. 51515.01(a) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2)).
Cost. The Legislative Analyst finds no direct state or local cost (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm)).
Signatures. Los Angeles County supplied 253,493 of the 918,358 raw petition signatures, about 28% (our calculation from the Secretary of State random sample count (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/1990-finalrandomsample-04-22-26.pdf)).
We found no City of Los Angeles analysis or position on the measure as of Sept. 30, 2026.
How it got on the ballot
Oct. 21, 2025: The Attorney General issued the petition’s title and summary. The proponent is Robert M. Hertzberg (Secretary of State, eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)), whom the Mercury News describes as a former Los Angeles assemblymember (Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/21/housing-ballot-measure-california-election/)).
Nov. 18, 2025: The campaign reported 25% of the signatures needed (Secretary of State, eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)).
Feb.-March 2026: Petitions with 918,358 raw signatures were filed with the counties (random sample count (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/1990-finalrandomsample-04-22-26.pdf)).
April 21, 2026: The random sample projected 715,233 valid signatures, more than 110% of the 546,651 needed, and the measure became eligible (random sample count (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/1990-finalrandomsample-04-22-26.pdf); Secretary of State, eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)).
Vote needed. A majority of votes cast statewide (Cal. Const., Art. II, Sec. 10 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2010.&article=II)).
Related measure. Proposition 1 on the same ballot is an $11.25 billion general obligation housing bond, repaid from the state General Fund, that includes about $1 billion for homebuyer assistance, the Mercury News reported (Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/21/housing-ballot-measure-california-election/)). Prop. 37’s conflict clause covers only another measure that authorizes revenue bonds for middle-class housing loans (text, Sec. 6 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=6)). See our Proposition 1 (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/measures/prop-01) page.
What each side says
In the state voter guide. The argument in favor was signed by Danny Curtin of the California Conference of Carpenters, Fiona Ma as a board member of CalHFA and David West of the California State Commanders Veterans Council. No argument against was submitted, so there are no rebuttals (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/arguments-rebuttals.htm)). The argument says:
Down payments: with a statewide median home price above $930,000, a 20% down payment can mean saving “over $186,000.”
Cost: “ZERO COST TO TAXPAYERS,” because private bond investors fund the loans and borrowers repay them.
Construction: helping buyers of new homes “will help accelerate construction.”
Consumer terms: “below-market, fixed-rate loans,” limits on lender fees and no prepayment penalty.
Arguments are the opinions of their authors and have not been checked for accuracy by any official agency (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Outside the guide.
Hertzberg said the goal is “to create generational wealth” and to help renters become owners. Proponents say it would lead to more than 190,000 new homes (Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/21/housing-ballot-measure-california-election/)).
The League of Women Voters of California opposes it, faulting the lack of clarity on rates and the absence of a first-time-buyer priority: “Prop. 37 does not meet that test” (Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/21/housing-ballot-measure-california-election/)).
KQED’s guide quotes the No argument that it “makes the state of California one of the biggest mortgage lenders in America overnight” and that “taxpayers are left holding the bag,” and lists Assemblymember Carl DeMaio in opposition (KQED (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-37)).
David Garcia of UC Berkeley’s Terner Center, which takes no positions, said it could help residents who qualify for a mortgage but lack savings, while “creating demand for builders to build new housing” (Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/21/housing-ballot-measure-california-election/)).
Checking the main factual claims against official records.
Claim Who makes it What official records show
Zero cost to taxpayers Yes campaign The Legislative Analyst finds no direct state or local cost (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm)). The bonds must state they are not a state debt (text, Sec. 51515.06(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5))
Below-market, fixed-rate loans Yes campaign The loans must be fixed-rate (text, Sec. 51515.04(a) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3)). The text tells CalHFA to set rates “practical and favorable to applicants” while covering bond costs, but sets no rate (text, Sec. 51515.05(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5)). The Legislative Analyst says what the loans would cost buyers compared with other options is unknown (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm))
Will accelerate construction; 190,000 homes Yes campaign The Legislative Analyst lists “whether the program results in increased home construction and homebuying” as unknown (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm))
Annual audits Yes campaign The text requires an independent annual audit (Sec. 51515.05(g) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5))
Taxpayers are left holding the bag No side (KQED) See the first row. The Orange County Register editorial, which opposes the measure, says “taxpayers have no direct risk” and that bond investors bear losses on these second mortgages (OC Register (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/20/endorsement-no-on-proposition-37-a-risky-25-billion-housing-experiment/))
Who supports and opposes it
Supporters
California Conference of Carpenters, State Treasurer Fiona Ma, the California State Commanders Veterans Council and United Nurses Associations of California (ballot label (https://content.lavote.gov/docs/rrcc/documents/final-measures-appearing-on-the-ballot-8-20-2026-v-12.pdf); argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
State Controller Malia Cohen, quoted in the argument in favor, and the California Teachers Association, named there as a supporter (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
California Association of Realtors and the Veterans Affiliated Council; Democratic candidate for governor Xavier Becerra (KQED (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-37)).
California Democratic Party, whose executive board endorsed the $25 billion down payment program on Aug. 2 (LA Times (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2026-08-02/california-democratic-party-endorses-prop-40-billionaire-tax)).
Opponents
League of Women Voters of California (Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/21/housing-ballot-measure-california-election/)).
Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (KQED (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-37)). His Reform California committee reported $33,000 in independent spending against Prop. 37 through Oct. 25 (Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip)).
No opposition committee has registered (Secretary of State totals (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-37-creates-loan-program-middle-income-buyers-qualified-new-homes-initiative-statute); Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/21/housing-ballot-measure-california-election/)).
Editorial boards. The Daily News and Orange County Register recommend no (OC Register (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/20/endorsement-no-on-proposition-37-a-risky-25-billion-housing-experiment/); Daily News (https://www.dailynews.com/2026/09/20/endorsement-no-on-proposition-37-a-risky-25-billion-housing-experiment/)). The San Diego Union-Tribune also recommends no: “Voting no on Proposition 37 is a good start” (San Diego Union-Tribune, Oct. 2, 2026 (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/10/02/endorsements-props-2-37-wouldnt-yield-saner-state-budgets-more-housing/)). The Mercury News and East Bay Times editorial boards recommend no on Propositions 1 and 37. They say Prop. 37 is “a creative way to help Californians take on more debt” (Mercury News, Oct. 26, 2026 (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/26/endorsement-proposition-1-37-affordable-housing-crisis-november-3-general-election/))

Proposition 37 : State loans for middle-income buyers of new homes
Published September 29, 2026 · Updated November 2, 2026
Proposition 37 would let the California Housing Finance Agency sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund a new down payment loan program. Loans could cover up to 17% of the price of a newly built home, and buyers would put down at least 3%. Buyers must live in the home, be state residents and earn no more than twice their area's typical income. Homeowners' loan payments, not the state, would repay the bonds.

Bond limit $25 billion in revenue bonds, repaid by borrowers
Loan size Up to 17% of the price; buyer puts down at least 3%
Top price in LA County About $1.56 million in 2026 (our calculation from federal loan limits)
Who can borrow One-year state residents, living in the home, earning up to 200% of area median income; first-time buyers not required
Cost to taxpayers No direct state or local cost (Legislative Analyst)
Money raised, Jan. 1, 2025 to Nov. 1, 2026 For: $28.0 million, including $3.9 million in late contributions after Oct. 17. Against: no committee
Largest donors California Association of Realtors committees, $18.76 million; Building a Better California, $6 million
Latest public poll PPIC, Oct. 16-22: 65% yes, 32% no (likely voters)
Each figure is sourced in the sections below. Money figures are our totals from the committees' state campaign reports.
Details and source links: Polls , Money for and against , What it costs , Sources .
What does a yes vote on Proposition 37 mean?
The state would create a new homebuying assistance program. The state could sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund the program. Bonds would be paid back by homeowners' payments on their home loans.
What does a no vote on Proposition 37 mean?
The state would not be required to create a new homebuying assistance program.
What would Proposition 37 cost?
The Legislative Analyst says there would be no direct state or local costs, because homebuyers' payments would repay the bond investors. How big the program gets depends on investor demand, how the loans compare with other options and whether it leads to more building and buying.
What it means for the City of LA
Homes in Los Angeles County would qualify up to a price of about $1.56 million, 125% of the county's 2026 federal conforming loan limit of $1,249,125 (our calculation). Only newly built or newly converted homes sold to their first buyer qualify. The City's own down payment programs serve first-time buyers and lower incomes; Prop. 37 would reach households earning up to twice the area median income. The Legislative Analyst finds no direct cost to the City or any local government.
The details
Official title Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes. Initiative Statute.
Type Initiative statute, placed on the ballot by petition signatures
Votes needed to pass Simple majority (more than 50% yes) of votes cast statewide
The question on your ballot
Authorizes $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of purchase price of a newly constructed home priced below about $1.5 million. Borrowers must be California residents, occupy the home, meet income limits, and pay at least 3% down. Bonds repaid by mortgage payments, not State. Fiscal Impact: No direct state or local costs. Supporters: United Nurses Associations of California; California Conference of Carpenters; California State Treasurer Fiona Ma Opponents: None submitted
What would change
Today If Proposition 37 passes
State down payment help The California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) runs a few down payment loan programs for low- and moderate-income buyers (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm)). Its Dream For All program lent up to $150,000 or 20% of the price to first-time buyers, with about $150 million to $200 million for its 2026 round and 14,000 applicants, the Orange County Register reported (OC Register (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/05/15/14000-apply-for-californias-housing-down-payment-program/)) A new “middle-class home ownership loan” funded by up to $25 billion in CalHFA revenue bonds (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm); text, Sec. 51515.06 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5))
Loan terms Not applicable A fixed-rate second mortgage for up to 17% of the price, behind the buyer’s first mortgage. The buyer puts at least 3% down from their own money. CalHFA sets the rate and terms at levels that repay the bonds and costs (text, Sec. 51515.05(b)-(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5); Sec. 51515.04 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3))
Who can borrow Not applicable California residents of at least one year who live in the home and earn no more than 200% of area median income for their family size. There is no first-time-buyer rule (text, Sec. 51515.01(a) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Which homes Not applicable New homes, townhomes, condos or manufactured homes, or units converted from nonresidential buildings, sold to their first buyer. The price may not exceed 125% of the county’s federal conforming loan limit (text, Sec. 51515.01(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3))
Lender fees Not applicable Origination fee capped at 0.5% or $290, whichever is greater. No prepayment penalty. Borrowers can ask to defer interest in a hardship (text, Sec. 51515.04 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=4))
Construction defect claims State law sets building standards and a process homeowners must follow before suing a builder (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm)) Builders who opt into a “qualified builder option” accept labor standards and liability for subcontractors’ wage violations. In return, their homes get different defect rules: builders may deal directly with owners, get releases after repairs and seek dismissal if owners stall for 120 days. Attorney contingency fees in defect cases over any qualifying home are capped at 30% unless a court allows more (text, Secs. 51515.02 and 51515.04(e) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=4))
Oversight Not applicable An independent annual audit of the program (text, Sec. 51515.05(g) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5))
Changes later Not applicable The Legislature may amend the act by more than a 60% vote of each house if the change furthers its purposes (text, Sec. 3 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5))
Each bond must state that it is not a debt of the State of California and is payable only from program funds (text, Sec. 51515.06(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5)). The measure does not set an interest rate for borrowers.
What it would mean in the City of Los Angeles
Price limit. The 2026 federal conforming loan limit for a one-unit home in Los Angeles County is $1,249,125 (FHFA (https://www.fhfa.gov/document/d/cll/fullcountyloanlimitlist2026_hera-based_final_flat.csv)). At 125% of that, a qualifying home could cost up to about $1,561,406, and a 17% loan on a home at that price would be about $265,439 (our calculations). The limit changes each year with the federal figure (text, Sec. 51515.01(b)(2) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3)).
New homes only. Resales do not qualify. Only new construction and conversions of nonresidential buildings sold to their first buyer do (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3)).
Compared with City programs. The City’s Moderate Income Purchase Assistance program lends up to $115,000 to first-time buyers, requires 1% down and a 660 credit score, and takes a share of the home’s appreciation (LA Housing Department (https://housing.lacity.gov/housing/help-moderate-income-first-home-buyers)). The Measure ULA-funded Homeownership Opportunities Program is limited to households at or below 80% of area median income (LA Housing Department (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula-homeownership)). Prop. 37 would reach households up to 200% of area median income and would not require a first purchase (text, Sec. 51515.01(a) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2)).
Cost. The Legislative Analyst finds no direct state or local cost (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm)).
Signatures. Los Angeles County supplied 253,493 of the 918,358 raw petition signatures, about 28% (our calculation from the Secretary of State random sample count (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/1990-finalrandomsample-04-22-26.pdf)).
We found no City of Los Angeles analysis or position on the measure as of Sept. 30, 2026.
How it got on the ballot
Oct. 21, 2025: The Attorney General issued the petition’s title and summary. The proponent is Robert M. Hertzberg (Secretary of State, eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)), whom the Mercury News describes as a former Los Angeles assemblymember (Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/21/housing-ballot-measure-california-election/)).
Nov. 18, 2025: The campaign reported 25% of the signatures needed (Secretary of State, eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)).
Feb.-March 2026: Petitions with 918,358 raw signatures were filed with the counties (random sample count (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/1990-finalrandomsample-04-22-26.pdf)).
April 21, 2026: The random sample projected 715,233 valid signatures, more than 110% of the 546,651 needed, and the measure became eligible (random sample count (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/1990-finalrandomsample-04-22-26.pdf); Secretary of State, eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)).
Vote needed. A majority of votes cast statewide (Cal. Const., Art. II, Sec. 10 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2010.&article=II)).
Related measure. Proposition 1 on the same ballot is an $11.25 billion general obligation housing bond, repaid from the state General Fund, that includes about $1 billion for homebuyer assistance, the Mercury News reported (Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/21/housing-ballot-measure-california-election/)). Prop. 37’s conflict clause covers only another measure that authorizes revenue bonds for middle-class housing loans (text, Sec. 6 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=6)). See our Proposition 1 (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/measures/prop-01) page.
What each side says
In the state voter guide. The argument in favor was signed by Danny Curtin of the California Conference of Carpenters, Fiona Ma as a board member of CalHFA and David West of the California State Commanders Veterans Council. No argument against was submitted, so there are no rebuttals (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/arguments-rebuttals.htm)). The argument says:
Down payments: with a statewide median home price above $930,000, a 20% down payment can mean saving “over $186,000.”
Cost: “ZERO COST TO TAXPAYERS,” because private bond investors fund the loans and borrowers repay them.
Construction: helping buyers of new homes “will help accelerate construction.”
Consumer terms: “below-market, fixed-rate loans,” limits on lender fees and no prepayment penalty.
Arguments are the opinions of their authors and have not been checked for accuracy by any official agency (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Outside the guide.
Hertzberg said the goal is “to create generational wealth” and to help renters become owners. Proponents say it would lead to more than 190,000 new homes (Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/21/housing-ballot-measure-california-election/)).
The League of Women Voters of California opposes it, faulting the lack of clarity on rates and the absence of a first-time-buyer priority: “Prop. 37 does not meet that test” (Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/21/housing-ballot-measure-california-election/)).
KQED’s guide quotes the No argument that it “makes the state of California one of the biggest mortgage lenders in America overnight” and that “taxpayers are left holding the bag,” and lists Assemblymember Carl DeMaio in opposition (KQED (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-37)).
David Garcia of UC Berkeley’s Terner Center, which takes no positions, said it could help residents who qualify for a mortgage but lack savings, while “creating demand for builders to build new housing” (Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/21/housing-ballot-measure-california-election/)).
Checking the main factual claims against official records.
Claim Who makes it What official records show
Zero cost to taxpayers Yes campaign The Legislative Analyst finds no direct state or local cost (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm)). The bonds must state they are not a state debt (text, Sec. 51515.06(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5))
Below-market, fixed-rate loans Yes campaign The loans must be fixed-rate (text, Sec. 51515.04(a) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3)). The text tells CalHFA to set rates “practical and favorable to applicants” while covering bond costs, but sets no rate (text, Sec. 51515.05(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5)). The Legislative Analyst says what the loans would cost buyers compared with other options is unknown (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm))
Will accelerate construction; 190,000 homes Yes campaign The Legislative Analyst lists “whether the program results in increased home construction and homebuying” as unknown (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm))
Annual audits Yes campaign The text requires an independent annual audit (Sec. 51515.05(g) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5))
Taxpayers are left holding the bag No side (KQED) See the first row. The Orange County Register editorial, which opposes the measure, says “taxpayers have no direct risk” and that bond investors bear losses on these second mortgages (OC Register (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/20/endorsement-no-on-proposition-37-a-risky-25-billion-housing-experiment/))
Who supports and opposes it
Supporters
California Conference of Carpenters, State Treasurer Fiona Ma, the California State Commanders Veterans Council and United Nurses Associations of California (ballot label (https://content.lavote.gov/docs/rrcc/documents/final-measures-appearing-on-the-ballot-8-20-2026-v-12.pdf); argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
State Controller Malia Cohen, quoted in the argument in favor, and the California Teachers Association, named there as a supporter (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
California Association of Realtors and the Veterans Affiliated Council; Democratic candidate for governor Xavier Becerra (KQED (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-37)).
California Democratic Party, whose executive board endorsed the $25 billion down payment program on Aug. 2 (LA Times (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2026-08-02/california-democratic-party-endorses-prop-40-billionaire-tax)).
Opponents
League of Women Voters of California (Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/21/housing-ballot-measure-california-election/)).
Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (KQED (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-37)). His Reform California committee reported $33,000 in independent spending against Prop. 37 through Oct. 25 (Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip)).
No opposition committee has registered (Secretary of State totals (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-37-creates-loan-program-middle-income-buyers-qualified-new-homes-initiative-statute); Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/21/housing-ballot-measure-california-election/)).
Editorial boards. The Daily News and Orange County Register recommend no (OC Register (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/20/endorsement-no-on-proposition-37-a-risky-25-billion-housing-experiment/); Daily News (https://www.dailynews.com/2026/09/20/endorsement-no-on-proposition-37-a-risky-25-billion-housing-experiment/)). The San Diego Union-Tribune also recommends no: “Voting no on Proposition 37 is a good start” (San Diego Union-Tribune, Oct. 2, 2026 (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/10/02/endorsements-props-2-37-wouldnt-yield-saner-state-budgets-more-housing/)). The Mercury News and East Bay Times editorial boards recommend no on Propositions 1 and 37. They say Prop. 37 is “a creative way to help Californians take on more debt” (Mercury News, Oct. 26, 2026 (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/26/endorsement-proposition-1-37-affordable-housing-crisis-november-3-general-election/))
